repos.title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
repos.paper_summary:
3DCodeVerse is an ecosystem for 3D coding agents with three parts: 3DCodeVerse-2M, a dataset of 2.03 M standalone executable 3D programs with their assets and verification records; a multi-agent harness; and open-model baselines. Programs come from public sources, converted representations (such as DeepCAD sequences translated to CadQuery), and harness-generated code. The harness splits a request into a directed acyclic graph of coding and assembly tasks, executes the output, checks geometry (bounding boxes, contacts, collisions), and has a VLM judge score renders against rubric criteria. Feedback drives repeated revisions without human input.

On 100 text-to-3D object prompts, human evaluators preferred the harness over each model's native harness in 69% to 89% of comparisons. Against Claude Design, both using Claude Opus 5.5, the harness won 90% of human comparisons (Judge Score 88 vs. 37). Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B raised the 3DCodeBench execution rate from 0.0% to 84.9%; Qwen3.8-27B rose from 51.9% to 92.9% with SFT and DPO.

Limitations: the object, scene, and graphics comparisons use 100, 50, and 50 prompts; rubric scores come from a VLM judge; and the fine-tuning results use one decoding seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: 3DCodeVerse combines a curated executable 3D code dataset with a harness that verifies and revises generated programs.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior 3D code work covers datasets, benchmarks and feedback harnesses, but these remain fragmented across tasks and environments.

digest_headlines.heading: 3DCodeVerse-2M: A large-scale 3D coding dataset
digest_headlines.headline: 3DCodeVerse-2M packages standalone executable 3D programs with assets, captions and separate verification records.

digest_headlines.heading: 3DCodeVerse Harness: A Data Engine for 3D Coding
digest_headlines.headline: The harness uses a multi-agent graph with execution, spatial and visual feedback to revise programs without human input.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Harness outputs win most human comparisons, reaching 90% against Claude Design, and fine-tuning raises execution rates.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of 3D coding
digest_headlines.headline: Code renders pass a door-and-handle geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 for a frozen video world-action model.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors plan to release datasets, harness, models and training recipes after reporting open-model and harness results.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix details harness runtimes, planning, judge scoring, a recorded run, articulation checks and a video-model comparison.

repos.title: Reactive Optimizers
repos.paper_summary: Reactive Optimizers presents OPAL, a method in which a pretrained language-model agent watches one training run and rewrites executable optimizer code (`updater.py`) and its own diagnostic program (`analysis.py`) during training, with no meta-training or cross-run memory. Across language modeling and image generation settings where no recipe was tuned, OPAL matches or beats the selected fixed recipes. On Goldfish Amharic, bits per sentence on FLORES-200 fall from 83.48 for the official recipe to 81.11 for OPAL. On LightningDiT-XL/1, FID-50K with guidance drops from 2.18 to 1.83. In a CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 run with 10% wrong labels, OPAL reaches test loss 0.685 against 2.493 for final AdamW weights. Changes include mid-run learning-rate increases, switching some matrices to Muon, and keeping one embedding matrix in float32. Wall-clock overhead is 1.01× to 1.14× when training does not wait for the agent. Limitations stated by the authors: gains are smaller on the heavily tuned modded-nanogpt task, and reactive edits may reduce reproducibility. Most runs were done once or three times.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed optimizer recipes cannot respond to training incidents, so the paper proposes an optimizer that rewrites itself during one run.

digest_headlines.heading: Training without a recipe
digest_headlines.headline: Without tuned recipes, OPAL matches or beats the best baseline in every new setting tested, including Amharic at 81.11 against 83.48.

digest_headlines.heading: Updating with spontaneous analysis
digest_headlines.headline: OPAL writes two programs: one rewrites the update code, and one chooses which training statistics to observe during the run.

digest_headlines.heading: What is dynamically changing during optimization?
digest_headlines.headline: Logged decisions show OPAL changing learning-rate schedules, optimizer assignments, precision, momentum, clipping, and data gating during training.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-world applicability
digest_headlines.headline: Letting training continue while the agent reasons adds 1.01× to 1.14× wall-clock time, and gains shrink on short, tuned runs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Most runs ended ahead of their starting recipes, and the authors argue reactive optimizers suit settings where no recipe exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists related work on learned and adaptive optimizers, the overfitting setup, and decision records for the runs.

repos.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Memorilla is a memory system that gives a frozen LLM query-dependent access to a document collection by supplying a fixed number of soft memory tokens in its input embedding space. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder stores each document once, and a trainable module uses query-conditioned slots and Perceiver-style cross-attention over all stored embeddings to produce K=16 tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Training runs in three stages (Wikipedia paraphrase reconstruction, ten reading and QA datasets, then the eight evaluation benchmarks) using negative log-likelihood on answer tokens only.

Across eight benchmarks covering personalization, long-document QA and knowledge-intensive QA, the paper reports the best average performance among compared methods, including full context, RAG-50, MemoRAG, Mem0, xRAG and LLMLingua-2. On FactKG, accuracy is 84.33% versus 80.43% for full context, using 108× fewer document tokens. In TextWorld, RL training of the memory module raises success from 18.6% to 24.2% over full-history in-context learning.

Stated limitations: the encoder was not trained for compression, so fine-grained factual details can be lost, and experiments cover only one Qwen encoder-decoder pair and no coding domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla gives a frozen LLM 16 query-dependent memory tokens built from a whole document collection instead of retrieved text.

digest_headlines.heading: Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Documents are encoded once, and a trainable module maps each query to K=16 soft memory tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla is compared with retrieval, compression and memory baselines on eight benchmarks using a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Quantitative Results
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla has the highest average score and leads on five of eight benchmarks, with a baseline ahead on NarrativeQA, PersonalizationV4 and PubMedQA.

digest_headlines.heading: What Does Memorilla Learn?
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla's advantage over retrieval-augmented generation (RAG-50) grows with entity count, while retrieval wins on who and which questions in NarrativeQA.

digest_headlines.heading: Continual Learning with Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Reinforcement-trained memory on TextWorld raises the average solve rate and cuts rollouts that exhaust the token budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The learned memory interface can serve growing histories with a fixed token count, but it can lose fine-grained factual details.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data and configuration, benchmark details, memory-token ablations and the TextWorld reinforcement-learning setup.

repos.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
repos.paper_summary: uni-robot-agent is a unified, modular harness that lets open-weight models act as robot-use agents in simulation and on physical robots. It gives agents shared tools with common units and feedback across environments through per-environment adapters, overlaps model reasoning with tool execution, and binds images, calibration, and robot state to immutable snapshots. On RoboDojo's 42 simulation tasks (252 episodes), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the harness scores 31.39 with 25.00% success. This is above the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and the listed VLA and WAM baselines, and the agent receives no simulator depth or task-verifier feedback. On 19 real-world tabletop tasks it scores 49.50, above Dream-1 (35.50) and close to a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ (47.75). Limitations: real-world agents receive RealSense depth while $\pi_{0.5}$ and Dream-1 use RGB only; precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain weak, and Qwen and DeepSeek trail Xiaomi-Robotics-1 and OpenWAM-$\alpha$ on long-horizon tasks. Trajectory analysis finds four failure patterns, which the authors link to visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Proprietary models block robot-use training, so this paper offers an open, trainable harness that reaches competitive scores.

digest_headlines.heading: uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Shared tools, five logical layers, and six design choices let agents run without simulator depth or verifier feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 31.39 Score on RoboDojo and 49.50 on 19 real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents?
digest_headlines.headline: Robot use appears across model generations and families, and four failure types suggest joint training targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Privileged Information
digest_headlines.headline: Removing camera parameters drops Qwen to 9.13, while removing skills changes Score from 31.39 to 30.31.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Cost and Speed
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen costs 1.09 USD per episode for 31.39 Score, and pipelining cuts episode time on all five tested tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robot-use harnesses offer varied tools and interfaces, so this work separates shared tools from model runtimes.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: An open-weight model with the harness reaches 31.39 Score, while precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain open.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists baselines, real-world task catalogue and scoring rules, per-task results, and agent case studies.

repos.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
repos.paper_summary: FlexGlue is a neural matcher that takes a set of query keypoints in one image and predicts their subpixel correspondences in the second image, while also predicting whether the pair is covisible so that non-overlapping pairs are rejected. A CNN backbone (frozen ConvNeXt-B with DINOv3 weights) produces a coarse token grid for each image. A 9-layer Transformer with self- and cross-attention updates the tokens, and a per-layer covisibility head can stop inference early on non-overlapping pairs. Each query gets a coarse position from a windowed softmax over cosine similarities, then a learned sub-cell offset. The model is trained on eight datasets with a joint correspondence, matchability, and covisibility loss. The paper reports that FlexGlue performs similarly to LoMa on sparse relative pose, is competitive with RoMav2 at lower cost, and gets the highest HardMatch mAA@10px in the sparse-to-dense setting. It also reports gains on ETH3D and IMC2025 SfM, InLoc, and a new indoor doppelganger benchmark built from LaMAR. Limitations include zero-shot evaluation on indoor disambiguation, since no indoor training data exists, and the paper notes that dense matching lacks robustness on HardMatch.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse matchers are fast but detector-bound, dense matchers are costly, and both miss visual symmetries.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior matchers either inherit keypoint detector limits or add separate post-hoc disambiguation models; FlexGlue handles both in one network.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FlexGlue aggregates context over dense token grids and reads out subpixel correspondences only at query keypoints, with covisibility heads.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show FlexGlue is competitive with dense matchers on relative pose at lower matching time, and it improves disambiguation, especially indoors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims top accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks and on disambiguation and localization benchmarks, at competitive cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists inference cost, keypoint detector results, benchmark curation, training details, matching modes, and limitations such as correlated errors and depth-edge accuracy drops.

repos.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
repos.paper_summary: This paper defines State Integrity Collapse (SIC), where a model can restate a persistent constraint but stops applying it to later turns, and introduces StateTrack-Bench to measure it. Each dialogue sets one constraint, adds related distractor turns, and tests compliance at depths 3, 5, 7, 10, and 12 across five categories: numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical rules. Seven provider-pinned models produce 875 scored outputs. A GPT-5.4 judge at temperature 0 scores strict joint retention, which requires both the immediate task and the constraint to be satisfied. A forked branch asks each model to restate the constraint, which separates behavioral drift from declarative fade. Strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% (Gemini-3.1-Pro) to 100.0% (DeepSeek-v4-Flash). Integrity failures make up 88.6% of observed failures, or 84.4% without Gemini-3.1-Pro. Limitations: 25 probes per category limits statistical power, the judge is an LLM (human-human kappa 0.82 to 0.87 on 80 outputs), distractors are non-adversarial, each dialogue has one constraint, and the 50-turn results come from a 40-scenario pilot.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Models can restate a constraint yet stop applying it, and the paper measures this gap across dialogue depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers instruction following, dialogue state tracking, and long-context position effects, but not whether remembered constraints stay binding.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark and Metrics
digest_headlines.headline: Strict joint retention counts a response only when it meets both the immediate request and the persistent constraint.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Seven provider-pinned model snapshots are tested at fixed prompts and seeds, with a single GPT-5.4 judge.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: DeepSeek-v4-Flash scores 100.0% strict joint retention while Gemini-3.1-Pro falls to 62.4% and loses 10.0 points by turn 12.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Excluding Gemini-3.1-Pro, numerical constraints at depth 50 show 100.0% recall but 79.2% compliance.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Symbolic constraints fail silently, so retrieval alone is insufficient and monitoring should prioritize them.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent-state evaluation is necessary, since State Integrity Collapse remains the dominant failure even without the most brittle model.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include 25 probes per category, model-based judging, a 30-scenario pilot, cooperative distractors, and one constraint per dialogue.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Scenarios were team-authored with no personal data, and the main risk is misuse as a blanket model safety ranking.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, confidence intervals, temperature and prompt-variant checks, pilots, state anchoring costs, judge audits, and release details.

repos.title: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
repos.paper_summary:
SurveyGraph is a survey-generation pipeline built around a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) with 21 typed relations among papers, including extends, improves, and applies. The MEKG drives core-paper selection, hybrid outline generation, graph-aware retrieval, and section-level write-evaluate-refine synthesis. A four-layer inference engine creates the relations, and an evidence gate with AUC=0.75 filters semantic edges.

Across eight archived runs, graph-aware retrieval raises core-paper recall from 0.216 to 0.373 over flat lexical retrieval (sign test p=0.004). In a seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion has higher relation density than flat lexical retrieval at similar recall. Two annotators labeled 108 stratified edges (binary support $\kappa=0.64$), and 68.5% were supported-or-partial after adjudication, with extends lowest at 52.8%. Citation audits over 160 generated sentences found 80.6% anchored-or-partial. A SurveyBench collection-stage probe on four topics reached 0.521 mean reference coverage with an eight-paper budget.

Limitations: the human study covers three relation types from one domain cluster. The MVSS and StructSurvey comparisons are not same-backend reruns. The SurveyBench probes do not test outlining or writing.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Flat retrieval in survey generation misses how methods evolve, so SurveyGraph builds a typed method graph to recover that structure.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups survey generators, benchmarks and graph tools, and differs by using one method-entity graph across the full pipeline.

digest_headlines.heading: The SurveyGraph Framework
digest_headlines.headline: The framework builds a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph and reuses it for outlining, retrieval and narrative synthesis.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Framework
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation separates graph-native diagnostics, retrieval benchmarks, grounding audits and benchmark alignment into distinct levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Graph-aware retrieval raises core-paper recall from 0.216 to 0.373 across eight runs, with p=0.004.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims an auditable typed structure layer, while SurveyBench results remain collection-stage diagnostics.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: SurveyBench results are collection-stage probes, and edge validation rests on 108 edges from one domain cluster.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Ethical risk is mainly hallucinated citations, and claims were checked against archived artifacts before inclusion.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists artifacts, reproducibility audits, Qwen generation diagnostics, the SurveyBench probe, the evidence-gate threshold analysis and comparison boundaries.

repos.title: KITE: Retrieval as a Decision Procedure for Long-Term Conversational Memory
repos.paper_summary:
KITE is a vector-free memory framework that treats retrieval as a deterministic decision procedure over a governed knowledge index. Sessions become memory entries tagged with topics from a vocabulary that expands and consolidates under controlled rules, plus typed participant, entity, place, and event keys. At query time, an LLM compiles each question into a retrieval plan validated against the same index. Fixed lookup, filtering, and an explicit scoring policy execute the plan, and a sparse lexical channel recovers surface details such as rare names. If no indexed evidence satisfies the plan, the system returns no match.

On LoCoMo (1,540 questions), KITE reaches 93.5% LLM-as-a-judge accuracy, 0.4 points above EverMemOS, using 1.5k reader-context tokens on average. On LongMemEval-S (500 questions), it reaches 86.0%, 3.0 points above EverMemOS, using 1.6k tokens. With the memory store frozen, it outperforms dense, BM25, and hybrid retrieval on accuracy and recall. Removing typed facets lowers LoCoMo accuracy to 90.0%. A stated limitation is weaker performance on single-session preference questions (63.3% on LongMemEval-S), which the paper attributes to difficulty aligning indirect preference expressions with the index. The reader and judge are both gpt-4.1-mini.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Embedding similarity ranking does not show that retrieved memories meet a question's conditions, so the paper proposes KITE, a vector-free alternative.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans persistent memory systems, structured memory organization, and executable retrieval over stored evidence.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: KITE builds a governed topic index, compiles questions into plans over it, and executes them deterministically with fixed ranking.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: KITE reaches 93.5% on LoCoMo and 86.0% on LongMemEval-S, the highest overall accuracy among the compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Preference questions remain the stated limit, with future work on aligning indirect preference expressions across construction and compilation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the LLM usage statement, benchmark and metric definitions, baseline and implementation settings, vocabularies, and prompt templates.

repos.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
repos.paper_summary: DiffusionART is an online reinforcement learning algorithm for diffusion models that aggregates prompt rewards into a shared guidance direction to remove a hidden forward-reverse consistency force identified in DiffusionNFT. The paper proves that NFT’s joint positive-negative training cancels this force only partially, leaving a residual that destabilizes training unless stabilized by an exponential moving average (EMA) with task-specific tuning. DiffusionART instead computes a normalized reward-endpoint covariance per prompt and applies it as a velocity target on reverse-rollout states. A second update adds drift-adaptive restoration without EMA, and a trust-region mask limits excessive policy shifts. On HunyuanVideo-13B with equal visual and motion quality weights, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean rewards of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast using 12.0× and 11.7× fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards. For image-to-video generation, it reaches a motion quality score of 6 with 4.8× fewer GPU hours than Flow-GRPO-Fast. Limitations include reliance on black-box reward models and the need for ODE rollouts, which restricts applicability to differentiable reward settings.

repos.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
repos.paper_summary: InteractiveWorld is a simulator built on Isaac Sim for closed-loop interaction between an egocentric MLLM assistant and a human. InteractiveBench is a set of 120 multi-turn tasks in six categories: Guidance, Planning, Accessibility, Decision, Prevention, and Finding. The human is an MLLM agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro in the main experiments) that follows the assistant's guidance and issues one of 36 action primitives. A kinematically driven SMPL+H body performs navigation and manipulation. Success is checked automatically from final object states. Twelve models were evaluated as the assistant. Claude Fable 5.1 passes 41.7% of tasks, and all other models reach at most 33.3%. The best models reach 20.0% on Guidance and 25.0% on Planning, compared with 85.0% on Decision for the best model. With the same human agent, an oracle assistant passes all tasks. Perception and memory errors account for 70.4%–85.7% of first errors across models. The human is simulated by an MLLM rather than real people, and visual input per turn is capped at 32 frames.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Static video benchmarks cannot test whether interactive assistants help people, so the paper proposes a closed-loop simulated environment and benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: InteractiveWorld
digest_headlines.headline: InteractiveWorld models a human who follows assistant guidance, using kinematic body control, collision checks and 36 action primitives.

digest_headlines.heading: InteractiveBench
digest_headlines.headline: InteractiveBench has 120 human-reviewed tasks in six categories, scored by final simulator object states rather than answer matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: The strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, passes 41.7% of tasks, and the best models reach only 20.0% on Guidance and 25.0% on Planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: InteractiveWorld and InteractiveBench provide a verifiable foundation for developing and evaluating interactive MLLM assistants.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, simulator implementation, benchmark construction and metrics, extra analyses, human-executor validation and future work.
